blocks.text: If you have used MCP before, you have probably talked about the client and the server as if they were the whole story. But there is a specific, narrow role called the client that does very particular work, and understanding exactly what it does, and does not do, clears up a surprising amount of confusion about how MCP actually behaves in practice. This lesson takes the client apart piece by piece: what it is, where it lives, what it owns, and where its job ends.
1. What a Client Actually Is

blocks.alt: A host runs a client, which connects to a server

blocks.text: An MCP client is a piece of software that maintains one connection to one MCP server and speaks the MCP protocol on behalf of whatever application it is embedded in. It is not a separate program a user opens, and it is not the AI model itself. It is closer to a dedicated adapter, or a phone line, that exists purely to carry protocol messages back and forth between the application and a specific server.

This is a subtle but important distinction from how people casually use the word "client" in everyday software, where a client often means an entire application, like a web browser or an email client. In MCP terminology, the client is a much smaller, more focused component, usually just a library or module instantiated in code, not something with its own window or interface.

code.content:
# Conceptually, a client is an object with a narrow job
client = MCPClient(server_connection)
await client.initialize()          # perform the handshake
tools = await client.list_tools()  # ask the server what it offers
result = await client.call_tool("send_email", {"to": "a@b.com"})

blocks.text: A useful mental shortcut: if you can point at a running process, a browser tab, or an app icon, you are probably looking at a host, not a client. A client only becomes visible if you go looking inside the host code, as one of potentially several small connection objects it manages internally.
2. Where the Client Lives: Inside the Host

A client never exists on its own. It always lives inside a host, the larger application a person actually opens, like a chat app, an IDE, or an autonomous agent runner. The host creates clients, hands them a connection to a server, and then leans on them to carry out the actual protocol conversation.

Think of the host as a building and the clients as individual phone lines installed inside it, one line per outside party the building needs to talk to. The building itself decides who to call and what to say, but each phone line is a dedicated, dumb piece of infrastructure that just carries the conversation faithfully once dialed.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: If you are building an MCP powered application, you will write host logic that decides which servers to connect to and what to do with results, but the client code that speaks the wire protocol is usually a ready-made SDK component you configure, not something you reimplement by hand.

blocks.text: 3. One Client, One Server Connection

blocks.alt: A client connects one-to-one with a server

blocks.text: This is the single most important structural rule about clients: each client instance corresponds to exactly one connection to exactly one server. A client never juggles multiple servers at once, and it never shares its connection with another client. If a host needs to talk to three servers, it creates three separate client instances, one per server, full stop.

This one to one rule is what keeps the protocol simple. A client never has to ask "which server does this message belong to," because there is only ever one possible answer for any given client instance. All of the routing complexity, if a host is juggling many servers, lives one level up, in the host, not inside any individual client.

blocks.text: 4. Why Not Just One Client for Everything

It might seem more efficient to have a single client juggle connections to every server a host cares about, saving on object overhead. MCP deliberately avoids this design, and the reasons come down to isolation, session integrity, and simplicity of failure handling.

Each server connection carries its own negotiated capabilities, its own session state, and potentially its own transport, one server might be reached over standard input and output as a local subprocess, while another is reached over an HTTP based transport across the network.

Mixing all of that bookkeeping into a single shared client would mean every bug or crash risks corrupting state for every server at once, rather than being contained to the one connection that actually failed.

blocks.title: An analogy worth keeping
blocks.content: Picture a translator assigned to exactly one delegate at a diplomatic meeting. Sharing that same translator across every delegate at once, hoping they can juggle several conversations simultaneously without ever mixing up who said what to whom, is exactly the kind of confusion the one client per server rule avoids.

blocks.text: 5. The Client Core Responsibilities

blocks.alt: A client handles discovery, routing, and state management

blocks.text: Stripped down to its essentials, a client has four jobs: perform the initialization handshake with its server, keep track of what that server has declared it supports, send requests and notifications on behalf of the host, and hand back whatever the server responds with. Everything else in a client implementation is really just supporting detail around those four jobs.

items: Perform the initialize handshake and remember the negotiated protocol version and capabilities
Track session level state for its one server connection
Serialize host intentions, like "call this tool" or "read this resource", into correctly shaped protocol messages
Deserialize server responses and notifications and hand them back to the host in a usable form
Detect and surface connection level failures, like a dropped transport or a malformed message

blocks.text: 6. Managing Session State

Once a client finishes its handshake with a server, it does not forget everything and start fresh with every message. It holds onto session state for as long as the connection is alive: the negotiated protocol version, the server capabilities it learned during initialization, and often a cached list of the tools, resources, and prompts the server most recently reported.

This cached state is what lets a host ask "what can this server do" instantly, without a round trip, and it is also what a client must correctly invalidate when the server sends a notification saying its tool list changed. Getting session state management wrong, serving stale cached data after the server has changed, is one of the more subtle classes of bug in real MCP client implementations.

It is worth noting that session state lives only as long as the connection does. If a client disconnects and later reconnects to the same server, it runs a brand new initialize handshake and rebuilds its session state from scratch, it does not assume anything it learned last time still holds.
7. Translating Host Intentions into Protocol Messages

The host thinks in terms of intentions: "the model wants to call the send_email tool with these arguments" or "the user selected this resource to attach as context." None of that is a wire format. The client job is to take that intention and turn it into a correctly structured MCP message, with the right method name, the right parameter shape, and a fresh unique id if it is a request.

This translation step is where a lot of protocol correctness actually lives. A host should never need to know that calling a tool means sending a JSON-RPC request with method "tools/call" and a params object containing a name and an arguments field, that is the client encapsulating protocol detail so the host can stay focused on decisions, not wire formats.
8. The Client View of a Server: Discovery

Right after initialization, a client typically asks its server what it actually offers, calling list operations for tools, resources, and prompts. This discovery step is how a client, and by extension the host, learns the concrete menu of what this particular server can do, since a server declaring the capability "tools" during handshake only says tools exist in general, not which ones.

A well behaved client treats this discovered list as the source of truth and never assumes a tool exists just because a similar server elsewhere offered it. Two servers can both declare tool support and offer completely different tools, and the client discovery step is exactly what protects a host from guessing wrong.
9. Routing Model Requests to the Right Client

blocks.alt: A model goes through a router to the right client

blocks.text: When a host is connected to several servers at once, and the AI model decides it wants to call a tool, something has to figure out which client, meaning which server connection, actually owns that tool. This routing decision is made by the host, using the discovery information each of its clients reported, not by any single client, since no individual client knows anything about its siblings.

In practice a host commonly builds a lookup table mapping a tool name back to the client instance that reported it, so that when the model says "call send_email," the host can find the one client connected to the server that actually owns that tool and hand the call off to it.

blocks.text: 10. Client Lifecycle: Creation, Use, Teardown

A client instance has a clear lifecycle. It is created and handed a transport to a specific server, it performs the initialize handshake, it spends most of its life sending requests and receiving responses and notifications, and eventually it is torn down, either because the host is shutting down that connection deliberately or because the underlying transport failed.
10.1 A Minimal Lifecycle Sketch

Most SDKs expose this lifecycle as an explicit sequence of calls, often wrapped in a context manager or similar construct so that teardown happens automatically even if something goes wrong midway through use.

code.content:
async with connect_to_server(server_params) as client:
    await client.initialize()
    tools = await client.list_tools()
    result = await client.call_tool("run_query", {"sql": "select 1"})
    # connection is automatically closed when this block exits

blocks.text: 11. Error Handling and the Client Job When Things Go Wrong

When a server returns an error response, or the underlying transport drops unexpectedly, the client is the first thing to notice, and its job is to surface that failure to the host in a clear, structured way rather than swallowing it or crashing silently. A client should never quietly retry a failed operation on its own without the host asking it to, since the host, or the model, may want to decide differently depending on what failed.

Good client implementations distinguish between protocol level errors, like a malformed response the server sent, and application level errors, like a tool call that failed because of bad input, and they preserve that distinction all the way up to the host rather than flattening every failure into a single generic exception.

items: Protocol errors: a malformed message, a request the server could not parse at all
Application errors: a well formed tool call that failed for a domain reason, like invalid input
Transport failures: the underlying connection itself dropped before any response arrived

blocks.text: 12. Clients Are Not Smart: They Do Not Make Decisions

blocks.alt: A client is mechanical while the model decides

blocks.text: It is worth stating plainly, because it trips people up: a client does not decide anything on its own. It does not decide which tool to call, it does not decide whether a result looks reasonable, and it does not decide when to reconnect after a failure. All of those decisions belong to the host, and often ultimately to the AI model the host is running, with the client acting purely as a faithful messenger.

This separation of concerns is deliberate. Keeping the client dumb and mechanical makes it easy to trust and easy to swap out for a different implementation, since its entire job is well specified protocol mechanics, with none of the harder, more subjective judgment calls mixed in.
13. Client Implementations in Practice

In practice, you rarely write a client from scratch. The official MCP SDKs, available for languages including Python, TypeScript, and others, ship a ready made client class that already implements the handshake, message framing, and session bookkeeping described in this lesson. Building a host application usually means configuring and using that client class, not reimplementing its internals.

blocks.text: Because the handshake, message framing, and session bookkeeping are handled by the SDK, the code a host team actually writes tends to focus on the parts that are genuinely specific to their application: which servers to connect to, how to present discovered tools to the model, and what to do with results.
14. Security Boundary: What a Client Should Never Do

Because a client sits directly between a host and an external server, it forms part of the security boundary of the whole system. A well behaved client should never forward host level secrets, like credentials for unrelated systems, into a server that has not been granted access to them, and it should never blindly trust everything a server claims about itself without the host having a say.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If a server declares a capability that was never negotiated during initialization, a careful client implementation refuses to act on it rather than silently going along, since accepting undeclared capabilities would let a misbehaving or compromised server exceed the boundary the host agreed to.

blocks.text: 15. Multiple Clients, Multiple Servers: The Full Picture

blocks.alt: A host runs client 1 to server A and client 2 to server B

blocks.text: Put all of this together and the full picture looks like a hub and spoke arrangement: one host in the middle, a separate client object for every server it is connected to, and each of those clients maintaining its own private session with its own server. The host is the only component with a view across all of them at once.

This is exactly the structure that solves the integration problem MCP was built for. Adding a fourth server to a host that already talks to three others means creating one more client instance, wiring it to the new server, and letting discovery tell the host what it now has access to, no changes required to the three existing clients.
16. Client Timeouts and Cancellation

Real connections do not always respond promptly, and a client needs a policy for how long to wait before giving up on a request. Most client implementations let the host configure a timeout per request, after which the client treats the call as failed even if the server eventually does respond.

MCP also supports explicit cancellation, where the client can send a notification telling the server to stop working on a specific in flight request. This matters most for long running tool calls, where a user or model may change their mind partway through, and waiting for the original call to finish anyway would waste time and resources on both sides.
17. Comparing a Client to a Plain API Client Library

If you have used a typical REST API client library before, an MCP client will feel familiar in spirit but different in shape. A plain API client library usually wraps one fixed set of endpoints defined by whatever service it targets, and it has no real notion of a handshake beyond perhaps sending an API key.

An MCP client instead performs a real negotiation step first, discovers its target dynamically through list operations rather than relying on hardcoded endpoint knowledge, and stays aware of change notifications for as long as the session is open. The MCP client is less "call this fixed endpoint" and more "discover, then converse."

blocks.text: Worked Example

Imagine a coding assistant host connected to two servers: one wrapping a company database, one wrapping a ticketing system. The host creates two client instances, Client A for the database server and Client B for the ticketing server. During startup, both clients run their handshake independently and report back what each server offers.

When the model later decides to create a ticket, the host looks up which client owns the create_ticket tool, finds Client B, and routes the call there. Client A, the database client, is never involved and never even sees that request, exactly the isolation the one client per server rule is designed to guarantee.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a client as if it were the whole application, rather than the narrow, single server connection component it actually is.
Sharing one client instance across multiple servers to save on object overhead, which breaks session isolation and mixes unrelated failure modes together.
Letting a client make judgment calls, like silently retrying or picking a fallback tool, that should belong to the host or the model instead.
Forgetting to invalidate cached discovery data, like a stale tool list, after the server sends a change notification.
Assuming two different servers that both declare the same capability, like tools, must offer the same actual tools.
Accepting server behavior that was never negotiated during initialization, instead of treating undeclared capabilities as untrusted.

blocks.text: A quick gut check before shipping a client integration: could two servers be confused for one another anywhere in this code, and does any error get silently swallowed instead of surfacing to the host. If either answer is yes, that is worth fixing before it becomes a hard to reproduce production bug.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A client is a narrow, mechanical component living inside a host, dedicated to exactly one server connection, responsible for the handshake, session state, and translating host intentions into correctly shaped protocol messages. It never makes decisions on its own, and a host connected to many servers simply runs many client instances side by side, one per server, never one client juggling several at once.

With the client role clear, the next lesson turns to the other side of that same relationship: the host itself, the application a user actually opens, and how it orchestrates every one of these clients to give the AI model a coherent, unified set of capabilities to work with.
